platforms.title: Why Does One Mouth Sore Heal Fast and Another Won't?
platforms.meta_description: A sore in your mouth isn't always the same thing. How to tell a canker sore apart from a cold sore, which one is contagious, and how each is managed.
platforms.body_html:
Assuming any sore in or around your mouth is basically the same thing? The American Academy of Oral Medicine explains that canker sores and cold sores are entirely different conditions with different causes. One isn't contagious at all; the other is a viral infection that can spread through contact.

Why they show up in different places, for different reasons

A canker sore is a small, round ulcer that forms inside the mouth — on the inner cheek, tongue, or the soft tissue between the gums. It has nothing to do with a virus; the usual causes are minor injury from biting the cheek, stress, acidic foods, or a deficiency in iron or vitamin B12. A cold sore, on the other hand, comes from infection with herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1), a virus most adults already carry and that stays dormant until something like fatigue, fever, sun exposure, or stress reactivates it. It starts with tingling along the outer edge of the lip, then moves through a blister stage that pops and crusts over.

According to the American Academy of Oral Medicine, canker sores are linked to stress, mouth injury, acidic foods, nutrient deficiencies, and family history, while cold sore outbreaks are triggered by fatigue or fever, sun exposure, stress, and a weakened immune system.

How to tell them apart, and how to avoid spreading one of them

First, where it shows up. Inside the mouth's soft tissue points to a canker sore; the outer edge of the lip or skin around the mouth points to a cold sore.

Second, whether it's contagious. Canker sores can't spread to anyone else, but a cold sore can spread through contact while it's blistering, which is why kissing or sharing items during that stage is worth avoiding.

Most of the time, both heal on their own within one to two weeks. A saltwater rinse or a protective oral gel can ease a canker sore, while starting an antiviral cream or pill right at the tingling stage can shorten a cold sore's course. On the other hand, a canker sore that hasn't healed after two to three weeks, is unusually large, or keeps coming back often, or a cold sore that shows up near or inside the eye, needs prompt medical attention, since one near the eye can threaten vision.

A doctor can usually tell the two apart just by looking, without needing extra tests, since the location, appearance, and history are typically distinctive enough on their own. For cold sores that keep coming back several times a year, it's worth mentioning that pattern specifically, since a doctor may prescribe a daily antiviral to reduce how often outbreaks happen rather than only treating each one after it starts. Tracking roughly how often either kind shows up, and what seems to trigger it — a stressful week, a sunny weekend, a bout of acidic fruit — also makes it much easier to catch a pattern than trying to recall it from memory months later.

The takeaway: check the location and whether it's contagious before assuming any mouth sore is the same as the last one. Anything that lingers or appears near the eye is worth seeing a doctor about right away. This article is for general health information; consult a medical professional for diagnosis and treatment.
